title: Differentiable Simulation of Hard Contacts with Soft Gradients for Learning and Control
claim: Control synthesis shares one computational graph through a simulator, and gradients flow back through it to states, actions and parameters.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right flow, dashed colored backward gradient arrows looping over the top
description: A single-panel computational graph. On the left, three colored circles hold the inputs: state x_k in blue, action a_k in lavender, and parameters p in green. Black arrows lead from each into a central gray box labeled 'Simulator'. A curved arrow under the box is captioned 'collision detection & contact solver'. A black arrow leads from the box to a white circle x_{k+1}, then on to a circle L labeled 'Loss'. A gray circle holds the target x̃_{k+1}, and an arrow from it also points to L. Dashed backward arrows in blue, lavender and green run from the loss back to the three inputs. Colored gradient labels sit at the top: ∇_{x_k}L / ∇_{a_k}L / ∇_p L. The eye goes first to the central Simulator box, then to the dashed gradient arrows.
caption: Common computational graph for robot control synthesis.
abstract: Contact forces introduce discontinuities into robot dynamics that severely limit the use of simulators for gradient-based optimization. Penalty-based simulators such as MuJoCo, soften contact resolution to enable gradient computation. However, realistically simulating hard contacts requires stiff solver settings, which leads to incorrect simulator gradients when using automatic differentiation. Contrarily, using non-stiff settings strongly increases the sim-to-real gap. We analyze penalty-based simulators to pinpoint why gradients degrade under hard contacts. Building on these insights, we propose DiffMJX, which couples adaptive time integration with penalty-based simulation to substantially improve gradient accuracy. A second challenge is that contact gradients vanish when bodies separate. To address this, we introduce contacts from distance (CFD) which combines penalty-based simulation with straight-through estimation. By applying CFD exclusively in the backward pass, we obtain informative pre-contact gradients while retaining physical realism.
